introduction.definition: A cooling tower fan is a large, slow axial fan that draws air through an induced-draught tower. It runs inside a flared fan stack that recovers velocity pressure, and is driven by a motor outside the humid air through a drive shaft and a right-angle gearbox.
applications: Induced-draught counterflow and crossflow cooling towers

pressure.title: Fan lifts the air; the stack recovers velocity pressure
pressure.description: The induced-draught fan draws air through the louvres and fill, so the plenum below the fan is slightly below atmospheric pressure (typically ≈ 100–250 Pa of static pressure duty). Large fans turn slowly (tip speed usually ≤ ≈ 60 m/s for noise) and move very large volumes. The flared stack slows the leaving air, turning part of its velocity pressure back into static pressure, so the fan needs less power. Blade pitch is set to load the motor correctly; tip clearance to the stack should be small and even.

A cooling tower fan is a large, slow axial fan that draws air through an induced-draught tower.
It runs inside a flared fan stack that recovers velocity pressure, and is driven by a motor outside the humid air through a drive shaft and a right-angle gearbox.
Typical applications include induced-draught counterflow and crossflow cooling towers; air-cooled heat exchangers (similar fans).

script.narration: How the Cooling Tower Fan works.
The motor drives the shaft from outside the stack.
The gearbox turns the drive 90° and reduces speed.
The fan draws air up through fill.
The stack recovers pressure as air leaves.
The flow overlay traces the liquid from suction to discharge.
The induced-draught fan draws air through the louvres and fill, so the plenum below the fan is slightly below atmospheric pressure (typically ≈ 100–250 Pa of static pressure duty).

video_tutorials.title: Cooling Tower Fan — Maintenance

script.narration: Maintenance essentials for the Cooling Tower Fan.
Check vibration and unusual noise.
Check blade pitch, tip clearance and bolts.
Rebalance; replace blades/couplings.
Watch for high vibration: vibration trip. Common cause: blade imbalance, ice, loose bolts.
Watch for coupling failure: shaft not turning. Common cause: misalignment.
Record every inspection so trends — vibration, temperature, leakage and performance — can be compared over time.
